# A citation cannot assert more fidelity than its capture preserved

A claim that cites a captured source can be no better grounded than the capture step left it. Fidelity is fixed at ingest and is **non-increasing** downstream: no citation syntax, no locator type, no review gate can promote a passage to a grade its capture did not preserve. The only operation that raises fidelity is re-capture.

This is a claim about **fidelity**, not authority, and the two move in opposite directions — worth stating plainly, because [trace-extracted memory earns authority per operation, not at capture](./trace-extracted-memory-earns-authority-per-operation-not-at-capture.md) asserts the complement. *Authority* — how much weight a reader should give a claim — is earned by post-capture work: verify, abstract, consult. *Fidelity* — what grade of provenance evidence a passage carries, whether the source's own words or somebody's restatement — is spent at capture and never replenished. The two compose: capture sets a ceiling, and post-capture operations earn authority beneath it. A heavily verified rule can still rest on a second-hand passage; a pristine verbatim quote can sit unverified indefinitely.

## Capture is layered because it is forced to be

The layering is not a design choice — [a framework rule with a boundary-preserving rival is not an inherited constraint](./a-framework-rule-with-a-boundary-preserving-rival-is-not-inherited.md), and no rival capture design drops the layering while preserving the commitments the framework has already made. A long source cannot be captured verbatim into markdown at full fidelity, because the consumer's context window is finite and because copyright forces trims. Any framework whose consumer is an LLM and whose sources are real documents faces both; hosted providers' output filters on mass verbatim reproduction add a third barrier, but that one is provider-contingent rather than inherited. So a snapshot of a long source is not a copy — it is an *extraction*, and it stratifies:

- **Verbatim layer** — the source's own words, reproduced. A claim may quote, and a machine can string-match the quote back against the snapshot.
- **Paraphrase layer** — the snapshot's own-words summary of a passage. A claim may cite it, but must not use quotation marks, and verification requires going back to the authoritative artifact (the sibling PDF).
- **Second-hand** — the captured text is itself another party's restatement (a court restating a complaint; a news article quoting an order whose original is no longer served). The citation must name the intermediary, because the provenance chain has a party in the middle whose fidelity is an assumption.

## Why notation cannot repair it

The temptation is to fix provenance downstream — a richer citation format, a structured span locator, a stricter gate. It cannot work, and the reason is exact rather than merely practical. [A derived copy of recomputable truth must be checked or absent](./a-derived-copy-of-recomputable-truth-must-be-checked-or-absent.md) requires a *mechanical derivation rule* before a copy may be trusted. A verbatim-layer quote has one: substring match. A paraphrase-layer passage has no such rule — there is no mechanical comparison between a paraphrase and its source, only judgment. So marking a paraphrase-layer passage `verbatim` does not make it verbatim; it produces precisely the hand-maintained-and-trusted copy that rule forbids, with a stronger trust signal attached than the unmarked version would carry. Notation can *express* the fidelity bound. It cannot move it.

This is the citation-fidelity instance of a general rule: [history has one chance to become checkable](./history-has-one-chance-to-become-checkable.md). The one chance here is ingest, and what was not preserved verbatim then is permanently downgraded — recoverable only by returning to the authoritative artifact and capturing again.

## Corollary: a locator must carry the layer, not just the span

It follows that a source-span locator encoding only *position* is underspecified. **Two spans at the same file offset can differ in provenance quality by a full layer** — one lifted from the snapshot's verbatim block, one from its paraphrase summary. A position-only locator would render them identical, which is the one distinction a consumer of the citation most needs. Any locator design must encode the layer.

## Scope

Change the premise and the conclusion moves, which is where the claim earns its boundaries. If a source is short enough to capture losslessly — a tweet, a short abstract, a commit message — the layers collapse to one, the bound goes vacuous, and *position* becomes the binding constraint again. In that regime a structured span locator earns its keep; the corollary above is out of scope rather than in conflict with that design. The claim bites exactly where capture is lossy, which is to say wherever the sources are long.

The practical consequence is that provenance quality is decided *before any note is written*. If a passage will be load-bearing, it must be promoted into the snapshot's verbatim layer at capture time, or the author must return to the authoritative artifact and quote-mine it. Because the debt is fixed at ingest and visible in the citation, it can at least be made explicit and repaid deliberately rather than discovered later.

## Open Questions

- Does forum-thread or transcript sourcing — many small utterances rather than a few long papers — change the natural grain, since each utterance *is* losslessly capturable while the corpus is not?
- Fidelity is a ceiling on verification, but is it a ceiling on *usefulness*? A well-attributed paraphrase may serve a reader better than a verbatim fragment shorn of context.

---

Evidence for the layering and for the failure of naive `verbatim` marking comes from both epistack casebook work in the sibling `epistack-casebooks` repository and from [ADR 046](../reference/adr/046-verbatim-quotes-are-validated-against-their-cited-source.md): the shipped verbatim-quote checker, run over that corpus, found eighteen of eighty-seven `verbatim`-marked spans that did not appear in their cited snapshot, with no false mismatches on manual audit.

# Writing conventions for kb/reports/ (report collection)

## Purpose and scope

This collection contains analytical outputs, evaluation records, and local
operational evidence that are consumed as reports rather than as library
claims or system definitions. Placement here is justified by the output's
retention policy and consumer, not by its filename or by the fact that a tool
generated it.

A report belongs here only when a named operation consumes the report itself.
Transferable claims belong in `kb/theory/`; descriptions of the shipped system
and its decisions belong in `kb/reference/`; executable procedures belong in
`kb/instructions/`; and reasoning whose value is consumed by unfinished work
belongs in `kb/work/`.

## Policy areas

Every report artifact lives in exactly one first-level policy area:

| Area | Retention policy | Typical contents |
|---|---|---|
| `state/` | Ignored, one directory per producing workflow. Not disposable merely because it was generated: the owning workflow decides when an output may be removed, and the [state README](./state/README.md) states per workflow what deletion loses. | Review results, packets and runs; fix dispositions; ingest working directories; connect, critique, friction, premise-decomposition and promotion-candidate reports. |
| `retained/` | Durable report records kept with the project. Payloads are tracked. | Evaluation corpora, experiment reports, measurements, and exact records cited by later work. |
| `types/` | Collection-local structural contracts, not report payloads. | Optional project-authored report contracts; command-produced generic report types are global. |

The published site includes `retained/` and leaves out `state/`. Inside `retained/`, a subtree carrying a
`.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker is left out of the site as well as
validation; mark exact captures and trial bundles so, keeping the report that
interprets them published.

Do not put report payloads directly at the collection root. Moving an artifact
between policy areas is a change in its retention contract, not a filing-only
rename.

## Quality goal

Make the report sufficient for the operation that consumes it without making
it impersonate a durable knowledge claim. State the subject, inputs or source
state, method, result, and material limits to the degree needed to interpret
or reproduce the output. Record the model and prompt or instruction identity
when an LLM judgment is part of the evidence and the producing workflow does
not already retain them.

`state/` must satisfy the owning workflow's authority, integrity, and cleanup
rules. `retained/` must remain
understandable from a clean checkout without relying on ignored files.

## Titles, descriptions, and exact records

- Use a title that names the analysis, experiment, or result. A title such as
  "Report" does not distinguish the artifact.
- When frontmatter is present, write a retrieval-oriented `description` that
  identifies the subject and why the exact output is retained.
- Frontmatter-free Markdown is permitted for deliberate unstructured output.
- Preserve an exact capture when fidelity is the report's purpose. If a copied
  artifact carries another collection's local type only as captured data, put
  a `.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker at the capture-set root rather than
  presenting that copy as a live typed artifact of this collection.

## Maintenance semantics

- A state producer owns cleanup and states, in the state README, what deleting
  its output loses: nothing unique (rebuild from retained inputs), one paid
  judgment (rerun when needed) or current coverage, an unresolved disposition
  or decision evidence (preserve). Generated state may contain non-reproducible
  judgments or the only current disposition, so Git ignore status never
  licenses deletion.
- A retained report is changed according to its declared role. Correct a
  living report in place; preserve a dated or frozen observation as an exact
  record and create a new observation when the measured state changes.
- Local evidence notes are the one interpreted form `retained/` keeps as
  durable artifacts: a `types/note.md` artifact whose bounded inference
  concerns only Commonplace's own choices or their measured effects, beside
  the raw records it interprets. Its formal edges use this collection's labels
  below. An inference that keeps a free variable belongs in
  `kb/theory/evidence/`.
- If a report develops a transferable claim, binding rule, system premise, or
  unfinished-work lifecycle, extract that content to its proper collection.
  Do not broaden `retained/` into a second notes, reference, instructions, or
  workshop collection.

## Outbound links

Reports may inspect any project surface. Use relative Markdown links for live
navigation and state in prose why the target matters. Inline links may carry
ordinary evidential or procedural context. Footer-shaped formal edges use this
small authorized set:

| label | destinations | reader need |
|---|---|---|
| `derived-from` | sources, external | inspect the source material from which the report was produced |
| `is-evidence-for` | theory, reference, reports | inspect the durable claim, decision, or report record on which this output bears |
| `compares-with` | theory, reference, sources, reports | compare two artifacts on a named shared axis |
| `see-also` | any durable collection, external | inspect useful adjacent context when no stronger relation applies |

The destination collection separately decides whether it may author a
reciprocal edge. A formal edge into this collection targets `retained/`;
`state/` may be mentioned inline only as local operational context.

Tracked library artifacts must not depend on an ignored `state/` file being
present. Summarize the needed evidence in the tracked artifact or
promote the exact report to `retained/` first. Tracked artifacts may cite a
`retained/` report when the exact record is useful to their reader.

## Validation markers

The tracked `.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker at `state/` excludes its
data-bearing subtree from collection-scoped validation. The marker does not
hide files from ordinary discovery, and explicit validation of
one typed report still applies its type contract.

A file under `state/` may declare any valid type spec, including another
collection's local type. Workflows stage candidates there for other
collections, and a candidate must validate against its destination's contract.
The type spec itself stays in the owning collection's `types/` directory.
`retained/` does not share this exception.

## What does not belong here

- A generated explanation or synthesis whose claim should survive the run →
  `kb/theory/` or `kb/reference/` according to its consumer.
- A procedure named "report" because it produces one → `kb/instructions/`.
- Drafts, deliberation, and run traces consumed by an unfinished investigation
  → `kb/work/`.
- External source captures and their durable analyses → `kb/sources/`.
- Build outputs with no report consumer → their build cache, not `kb/reports/`.

# Review result

A review result records one assessment of captured target text against a criterion. Completion means the output passed deterministic checks, not that its judgment is correct. A report outcome is not a favorable verdict. Use this type for individual gate, compression-check, type-conformance and collection-conformance verdicts, and for critique, composition-friction, premise-decomposition and compression-synthesis reports and role reports. Do not use it for combined improvement packets or connection discovery.

## Content

Findings state what the assessed text establishes or fails to establish. Each passage finding quotes enough verbatim text to identify one contiguous span uniquely. A quote is matched after whitespace and typographic quote marks are normalized, so a line wrap in the target does not break it. A quote therefore identifies a passage and is not a byte-exact copy of it. A consumer that needs the exact span locates the quote in the captured target, which holds the exact bytes. A document-wide or absence finding explains the condition without inventing a quotation. Finding levels belong to verdict criteria; critique reports instead state whether the strongest attack lands and how the note engages it. An empty findings list is an honest completed result when no finding remains.

The body explains the assessment without repeating every structured finding. A critique preserves its central commitment, critique mode, strongest case, the note's response and constructive findings, including why an attack does not survive. Low-confidence no-surviving-attack findings leave the need for a domain check visible.

Each report method has its own shape, which the schema checks by the result's `criterion`:

| Method | Findings | Required body |
|---|---|---|
| Critique | constructive findings | `attack-outcome` in frontmatter; `## Strongest case against it`, `## How the note engages it`, `## Constructive findings` |
| Composition friction | the surfaced joints, thinnest first; each reason begins `UNSUPPORTED`, `THIN` or `HOLDS` | a `**Filter:** SURVIVES` or `DISSOLVES` line; `## Filter`, `## Thinnest joints`, `## For the human` |
| Premise decomposition | one per premise; each reason begins `HOLDS`, `DOUBTFUL` or `DEFEATED`, and a non-`HOLDS` reason names `LOCAL` or `GLOBAL` and `instance`, `prevalence` or `priced-exception` | a `**Register:**` line; `## Premises and counterexamples`, `## For the human` |
| Compression synthesis | zero to three opportunities | `## Opportunities` |
| Role report | one per dependent need, duplication or untaken recommendation; each reason begins `SUPPLIED`, `PARTLY SUPPLIED`, `NOT SUPPLIED`, `DUPLICATED` or `UNTAKEN` | `## Role`, `## Dependents`, `## Duplication`, `## Untaken recommendations`, `## Reach` |

Only critique supplies `attack-outcome`. Friction's filter line and the premise statuses route attention; they are not overall verdicts. A report criterion is named by its library instruction's identity, so moving one of these instructions requires a schema edit.

## Field ownership

The worker fragment supplies only `type`, `findings`, `outcome`, optional `attack-outcome`, and the body. Findings precede the outcome so the serialized verdict follows its rationale. The fragment is not a complete saved artifact. The controller completes and validates it; workers never assert hashes, execution identities or timestamps.

| Fields | Owner and meaning |
|---|---|
| `type`, `findings`, `outcome`, `attack-outcome` | Worker assessment; findings contain `scope`, `quotes`, `reason`, and `level` for verdicts |
| `description`, `format`, `contract` | Controller's result-format identity and expected verdict/report contract |
| `note`, `criterion` | Original target and criterion identities |
| `note-sha256`, `criterion-sha256` | Freshness hashes; the note hash may cover normalized watched parts, not exact bytes |
| `target-sha256`, `target-capture` | Exact assessed UTF-8 bytes and their retained repository-relative location |
| `observation`, `contract-sha256` | Execution observation and captured output-contract identity |
| `profile`, `model`, `run`, `launch`, `completed-at` | Requested execution configuration and observed execution provenance |
| `raw-output`, `raw-output-sha256` | Retained original worker fragment, distinct from this completed artifact |

## Template

Worker fragment for a verdict criterion; code supplies the remaining fields:

```markdown
---
type: types/review-result.md
findings:
  - scope: document
    quotes: []
    reason: "The claim omits the condition needed for its stated conclusion."
    level: warn
outcome: warn
---

# Review

## Summary

The conclusion needs its missing condition.
```

A critique fragment uses `outcome: report`, supplies `attack-outcome`, and omits finding levels. Its body retains the critique instruction's sections. Other report fragments use `outcome: report`, omit `attack-outcome` and finding levels, and follow their instruction's Output section. Neither fragment uses a terminal `## Result:` line. Operational production and publication belong to the review command, not to this type.

The note is `kb/theory/a-citation-cannot-assert-more-fidelity-than-its-capture-preserved.md` in this repository; its text is <Inputs: note.md>. The criterion is `kb/instructions/compression-bundle/marginal-value-redundancy.md`; its text is <Inputs: criterion.md>. Judge these input texts; the files on disk may have changed since.

This is one compression check. It reports PASS, INFO or WARN and has no FAIL.
Write PASS as outcome: pass; INFO as outcome: pass with info findings; WARN as outcome: warn.

Reading scope:
- The note's relative links resolve from `kb/theory/`. For grounding or consistency checks, read only files the note links to, except for one exact local path that the criterion explicitly tells you to derive from such a link.
- Ignore review backups, workshop copies and historical artifacts unless the note links to them.
- Never browse shared operational state or other runs, even through a link. Operational inputs must be supplied copies.
- Do not delegate or start another agent.

- Write the review to <Required outputs: review.md>. Write nothing else: create, edit or delete no file in the repository, and run no command that changes it or its git state.

- Each finding has scope: passage | document, quotes (verbatim target spans that occur once, empty for document scope;
  line wraps and quote-mark style are ignored when matching),

- The supplied review-result type and schema define the output contract. Supply only worker-owned fields;
  the controller supplies all provenance. Express findings once in frontmatter, not a second prose list.

# Critique a note

Build the strongest case that a note's central commitment is wrong, then check whether the note already answers it — and report honestly when the strongest available case does not survive. This is an open-ended, report-kind assay: it completes with a critique, not a PASS/WARN/FAIL verdict. `ERROR` reports inability to complete the assay and fails the job; a note that withstands the strongest attack is a completed critique, not an `ERROR`. Write the report; do not touch the note.

Run it in a **fresh sub-agent** (or a different runner than wrote the note) so the critic has no sympathy for the note's framing.

The caller owns reviewer lifecycle. After the report has been written and verified, close, terminate, or release the critic with the harness lifecycle operation. The critic is a single-use context and must not receive follow-up work.

## The critique

Attack the note's central commitment in the mode its artifact kind calls for — steelman the opposing position for a claim, find the counterexample or the idle distinction for a definition, show the wrong outcome for a procedure, find the discrepancy for a description.

Make the attack **maximally strong**: the version an informed opponent would actually make, named to a concrete stance — not a balanced "some might disagree." If the author could dismiss it in one sentence, it is not strong enough yet.

Constructing that attack has two honest outcomes. Usually the strongest objection **lands**, fully or partially, and the report presents it. But sometimes the strongest case an informed opponent could make is one the note already fully answers, or one that does not apply on inspection — that is a first-class result, **no surviving attack**, not a failure to complete. Do **not** escalate to a contrived, vague, or unfalsifiable objection to satisfy the format: an objection the author cannot dismiss *because it is slippery* is weaker, not stronger. "No surviving attack" is earned, not a default — you must still have built the strongest real objection, and you must name it and show exactly why it fails, so the finding is inspectable rather than a fluent "looks fine". Default to attacking hard; conclude no surviving attack only when the strongest objection you can build genuinely does not land. When reaching **no surviving attack** rests on domain knowledge you are not confident you have — a competent specialist might build an objection you could not — report it as **no surviving attack (low confidence — needs domain check)** rather than a clean result, so a reader escalates instead of treating the commitment as settled. This does not remove the limit that one critic cannot certify its own objection is the strongest; it makes that residual visible for the other review lenses and the human to catch.

## Report shape

The caller supplies the output destination and owns any surrounding protocol markers. When run through `commonplace-review`, write only the output file the run names; when run by hand, name a report path explicitly before dispatch. Mutate nothing else.

```markdown
# Critique: <note title>

**Note:** <path>
**Central commitment:** <one sentence>
**Critique mode:** <claim | definition | procedure | description>
**Attack outcome:** <lands | partially lands | no surviving attack | no surviving attack (low confidence — needs domain check)>

## Strongest case against it
<the strongest real objection — who holds it, why, and its best reasoning; state it even when the outcome is "no surviving attack", so the conclusion is inspectable>

## How the note engages it
<engaged | partially engaged | unengaged | fully answers, with where in the note>

## Constructive findings
- <what would let the note contend with the attack; "none — the note already answers the strongest objection" when the outcome is no surviving attack>

## Secondary objections (optional)
- <weaker but real objections worth noting>
```

---

Fidelity is fixed at ingest and is **non-increasing** downstream: no citation syntax, no locator type, no review gate can promote a passage to a grade its capture did not preserve. The only operation that raises fidelity is re-capture.

This is a claim about **fidelity**, not authority, and the two move in opposite directions — worth stating plainly, because [trace-extracted memory earns authority per operation, not at capture](./trace-extracted-memory-earns-authority-per-operation-not-at-capture.md) asserts the complement. *Authority* — how much weight a reader should give a claim — is earned by post-capture work: verify, abstract, consult. *Fidelity* — what grade of provenance evidence a passage carries, whether the source's own words or somebody's restatement — is spent at capture and never replenished. The two compose: capture sets a ceiling, and post-capture operations earn authority beneath it. A heavily verified rule can still rest on a second-hand passage; a pristine verbatim quote can sit unverified indefinitely.

## Capture is layered because it is forced to be

The layering is not a design choice — [a framework rule with a boundary-preserving rival is not an inherited constraint](./a-framework-rule-with-a-boundary-preserving-rival-is-not-inherited.md), and no rival capture design drops the layering while preserving the commitments the framework has already made. A long source cannot be captured verbatim into markdown at full fidelity, because the consumer's context window is finite and because copyright forces trims. Any framework whose consumer is an LLM and whose sources are real documents faces both; hosted providers' output filters on mass verbatim reproduction add a third barrier, but that one is provider-contingent rather than inherited. So a snapshot of a long source is not a copy — it is an *extraction*, and it stratifies:

- **Verbatim layer** — the source's own words, reproduced. A claim may quote, and a machine can string-match the quote back against the snapshot.
- **Paraphrase layer** — the snapshot's own-words summary of a passage. A claim may cite it, but must not use quotation marks, and verification requires going back to the authoritative artifact (the sibling PDF).
- **Second-hand** — the captured text is itself another party's restatement (a court restating a complaint; a news article quoting an order whose original is no longer served). The citation must name the intermediary, because the provenance chain has a party in the middle whose fidelity is an assumption.

## Why notation cannot repair it

The temptation is to fix provenance downstream — a richer citation format, a structured span locator, a stricter gate. It cannot work, and the reason is exact rather than merely practical. [A derived copy of recomputable truth must be checked or absent](./a-derived-copy-of-recomputable-truth-must-be-checked-or-absent.md) requires a *mechanical derivation rule* before a copy may be trusted. A verbatim-layer quote has one: substring match. A paraphrase-layer passage has no such rule — there is no mechanical comparison between a paraphrase and its source, only judgment. So marking a paraphrase-layer passage `verbatim` does not make it verbatim; it produces precisely the hand-maintained-and-trusted copy that rule forbids, with a stronger trust signal attached than the unmarked version would carry. Notation can *express* the fidelity bound. It cannot move it.

This is the citation-fidelity instance of a general rule: [history has one chance to become checkable](./history-has-one-chance-to-become-checkable.md). The one chance here is ingest, and what was not preserved verbatim then is permanently downgraded — recoverable only by returning to the authoritative artifact and capturing again.

## Corollary: a locator must carry the layer, not just the span

It follows that a source-span locator encoding only *position* is underspecified. **Two spans at the same file offset can differ in provenance quality by a full layer** — one lifted from the snapshot's verbatim block, one from its paraphrase summary. A position-only locator would render them identical, which is the one distinction a consumer of the citation most needs. Any locator design must encode the layer.

## Scope

Change the premise and the conclusion moves, which is where the claim earns its boundaries. If a source is short enough to capture losslessly — a tweet, a short abstract, a commit message — the layers collapse to one, the bound goes vacuous, and *position* becomes the binding constraint again. In that regime a structured span locator earns its keep; the corollary above is out of scope rather than in conflict with that design. The claim bites exactly where capture is lossy, which is to say wherever the sources are long.

The practical consequence is that provenance quality is decided *before any note is written*. If a passage will be load-bearing, it must be promoted into the snapshot's verbatim layer at capture time, or the author must return to the authoritative artifact and quote-mine it. Because the debt is fixed at ingest and visible in the citation, it can at least be made explicit and repaid deliberately rather than discovered later.

## Open Questions

- Does forum-thread or transcript sourcing — many small utterances rather than a few long papers — change the natural grain, since each utterance *is* losslessly capturable while the corpus is not?
- Fidelity is a ceiling on verification, but is it a ceiling on *usefulness*? A well-attributed paraphrase may serve a reader better than a verbatim fragment shorn of context.

---

Evidence for the layering and for the failure of naive `verbatim` marking comes from both epistack casebook work in the sibling `epistack-casebooks` repository and from [ADR 046](../reference/adr/046-verbatim-quotes-are-validated-against-their-cited-source.md): the shipped verbatim-quote checker, run over that corpus, found eighteen of eighty-seven `verbatim`-marked spans that did not appear in their cited snapshot, with no false mismatches on manual audit.

# Writing conventions for kb/reports/ (report collection)

## Purpose and scope

This collection contains analytical outputs, evaluation records, and local
operational evidence that are consumed as reports rather than as library
claims or system definitions. Placement here is justified by the output's
retention policy and consumer, not by its filename or by the fact that a tool
generated it.

A report belongs here only when a named operation consumes the report itself.
Transferable claims belong in `kb/theory/`; descriptions of the shipped system
and its decisions belong in `kb/reference/`; executable procedures belong in
`kb/instructions/`; and reasoning whose value is consumed by unfinished work
belongs in `kb/work/`.

## Policy areas

Every report artifact lives in exactly one first-level policy area:

| Area | Retention policy | Typical contents |
|---|---|---|
| `state/` | Ignored, one directory per producing workflow. Not disposable merely because it was generated: the owning workflow decides when an output may be removed, and the [state README](./state/README.md) states per workflow what deletion loses. | Review results, packets and runs; fix dispositions; ingest working directories; connect, critique, friction, premise-decomposition and promotion-candidate reports. |
| `retained/` | Durable report records kept with the project. Payloads are tracked. | Evaluation corpora, experiment reports, measurements, and exact records cited by later work. |
| `types/` | Collection-local structural contracts, not report payloads. | Optional project-authored report contracts; command-produced generic report types are global. |

The published site includes `retained/` and leaves out `state/`. Inside `retained/`, a subtree carrying a
`.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker is left out of the site as well as
validation; mark exact captures and trial bundles so, keeping the report that
interprets them published.

Do not put report payloads directly at the collection root. Moving an artifact
between policy areas is a change in its retention contract, not a filing-only
rename.

## Quality goal

Make the report sufficient for the operation that consumes it without making
it impersonate a durable knowledge claim. State the subject, inputs or source
state, method, result, and material limits to the degree needed to interpret
or reproduce the output. Record the model and prompt or instruction identity
when an LLM judgment is part of the evidence and the producing workflow does
not already retain them.

`state/` must satisfy the owning workflow's authority, integrity, and cleanup
rules. `retained/` must remain
understandable from a clean checkout without relying on ignored files.

## Titles, descriptions, and exact records

- Use a title that names the analysis, experiment, or result. A title such as
  "Report" does not distinguish the artifact.
- When frontmatter is present, write a retrieval-oriented `description` that
  identifies the subject and why the exact output is retained.
- Frontmatter-free Markdown is permitted for deliberate unstructured output.
- Preserve an exact capture when fidelity is the report's purpose. If a copied
  artifact carries another collection's local type only as captured data, put
  a `.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker at the capture-set root rather than
  presenting that copy as a live typed artifact of this collection.

## Maintenance semantics

- A state producer owns cleanup and states, in the state README, what deleting
  its output loses: nothing unique (rebuild from retained inputs), one paid
  judgment (rerun when needed) or current coverage, an unresolved disposition
  or decision evidence (preserve). Generated state may contain non-reproducible
  judgments or the only current disposition, so Git ignore status never
  licenses deletion.
- A retained report is changed according to its declared role. Correct a
  living report in place; preserve a dated or frozen observation as an exact
  record and create a new observation when the measured state changes.
- Local evidence notes are the one interpreted form `retained/` keeps as
  durable artifacts: a `types/note.md` artifact whose bounded inference
  concerns only Commonplace's own choices or their measured effects, beside
  the raw records it interprets. Its formal edges use this collection's labels
  below. An inference that keeps a free variable belongs in
  `kb/theory/evidence/`.
- If a report develops a transferable claim, binding rule, system premise, or
  unfinished-work lifecycle, extract that content to its proper collection.
  Do not broaden `retained/` into a second notes, reference, instructions, or
  workshop collection.

## Outbound links

Reports may inspect any project surface. Use relative Markdown links for live
navigation and state in prose why the target matters. Inline links may carry
ordinary evidential or procedural context. Footer-shaped formal edges use this
small authorized set:

| label | destinations | reader need |
|---|---|---|
| `derived-from` | sources, external | inspect the source material from which the report was produced |
| `is-evidence-for` | theory, reference, reports | inspect the durable claim, decision, or report record on which this output bears |
| `compares-with` | theory, reference, sources, reports | compare two artifacts on a named shared axis |
| `see-also` | any durable collection, external | inspect useful adjacent context when no stronger relation applies |

The destination collection separately decides whether it may author a
reciprocal edge. A formal edge into this collection targets `retained/`;
`state/` may be mentioned inline only as local operational context.

Tracked library artifacts must not depend on an ignored `state/` file being
present. Summarize the needed evidence in the tracked artifact or
promote the exact report to `retained/` first. Tracked artifacts may cite a
`retained/` report when the exact record is useful to their reader.

## Validation markers

The tracked `.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker at `state/` excludes its
data-bearing subtree from collection-scoped validation. The marker does not
hide files from ordinary discovery, and explicit validation of
one typed report still applies its type contract.

A file under `state/` may declare any valid type spec, including another
collection's local type. Workflows stage candidates there for other
collections, and a candidate must validate against its destination's contract.
The type spec itself stays in the owning collection's `types/` directory.
`retained/` does not share this exception.

## What does not belong here

- A generated explanation or synthesis whose claim should survive the run →
  `kb/theory/` or `kb/reference/` according to its consumer.
- A procedure named "report" because it produces one → `kb/instructions/`.
- Drafts, deliberation, and run traces consumed by an unfinished investigation
  → `kb/work/`.
- External source captures and their durable analyses → `kb/sources/`.
- Build outputs with no report consumer → their build cache, not `kb/reports/`.

# Review result

A review result records one assessment of captured target text against a criterion. Completion means the output passed deterministic checks, not that its judgment is correct. A report outcome is not a favorable verdict. Use this type for individual gate, compression-check, type-conformance and collection-conformance verdicts, and for critique, composition-friction, premise-decomposition and compression-synthesis reports and role reports. Do not use it for combined improvement packets or connection discovery.

## Content

Findings state what the assessed text establishes or fails to establish. Each passage finding quotes enough verbatim text to identify one contiguous span uniquely. A quote is matched after whitespace and typographic quote marks are normalized, so a line wrap in the target does not break it. A quote therefore identifies a passage and is not a byte-exact copy of it. A consumer that needs the exact span locates the quote in the captured target, which holds the exact bytes. A document-wide or absence finding explains the condition without inventing a quotation. Finding levels belong to verdict criteria; critique reports instead state whether the strongest attack lands and how the note engages it. An empty findings list is an honest completed result when no finding remains.

The body explains the assessment without repeating every structured finding. A critique preserves its central commitment, critique mode, strongest case, the note's response and constructive findings, including why an attack does not survive. Low-confidence no-surviving-attack findings leave the need for a domain check visible.

Each report method has its own shape, which the schema checks by the result's `criterion`:

| Method | Findings | Required body |
|---|---|---|
| Critique | constructive findings | `attack-outcome` in frontmatter; `## Strongest case against it`, `## How the note engages it`, `## Constructive findings` |
| Composition friction | the surfaced joints, thinnest first; each reason begins `UNSUPPORTED`, `THIN` or `HOLDS` | a `**Filter:** SURVIVES` or `DISSOLVES` line; `## Filter`, `## Thinnest joints`, `## For the human` |
| Premise decomposition | one per premise; each reason begins `HOLDS`, `DOUBTFUL` or `DEFEATED`, and a non-`HOLDS` reason names `LOCAL` or `GLOBAL` and `instance`, `prevalence` or `priced-exception` | a `**Register:**` line; `## Premises and counterexamples`, `## For the human` |
| Compression synthesis | zero to three opportunities | `## Opportunities` |
| Role report | one per dependent need, duplication or untaken recommendation; each reason begins `SUPPLIED`, `PARTLY SUPPLIED`, `NOT SUPPLIED`, `DUPLICATED` or `UNTAKEN` | `## Role`, `## Dependents`, `## Duplication`, `## Untaken recommendations`, `## Reach` |

Only critique supplies `attack-outcome`. Friction's filter line and the premise statuses route attention; they are not overall verdicts. A report criterion is named by its library instruction's identity, so moving one of these instructions requires a schema edit.

## Field ownership

The worker fragment supplies only `type`, `findings`, `outcome`, optional `attack-outcome`, and the body. Findings precede the outcome so the serialized verdict follows its rationale. The fragment is not a complete saved artifact. The controller completes and validates it; workers never assert hashes, execution identities or timestamps.

| Fields | Owner and meaning |
|---|---|
| `type`, `findings`, `outcome`, `attack-outcome` | Worker assessment; findings contain `scope`, `quotes`, `reason`, and `level` for verdicts |
| `description`, `format`, `contract` | Controller's result-format identity and expected verdict/report contract |
| `note`, `criterion` | Original target and criterion identities |
| `note-sha256`, `criterion-sha256` | Freshness hashes; the note hash may cover normalized watched parts, not exact bytes |
| `target-sha256`, `target-capture` | Exact assessed UTF-8 bytes and their retained repository-relative location |
| `observation`, `contract-sha256` | Execution observation and captured output-contract identity |
| `profile`, `model`, `run`, `launch`, `completed-at` | Requested execution configuration and observed execution provenance |
| `raw-output`, `raw-output-sha256` | Retained original worker fragment, distinct from this completed artifact |

## Template

Worker fragment for a verdict criterion; code supplies the remaining fields:

```markdown
---
type: types/review-result.md
findings:
  - scope: document
    quotes: []
    reason: "The claim omits the condition needed for its stated conclusion."
    level: warn
outcome: warn
---

# Review

## Summary

The conclusion needs its missing condition.
```

A critique fragment uses `outcome: report`, supplies `attack-outcome`, and omits finding levels. Its body retains the critique instruction's sections. Other report fragments use `outcome: report`, omit `attack-outcome` and finding levels, and follow their instruction's Output section. Neither fragment uses a terminal `## Result:` line. Operational production and publication belong to the review command, not to this type.

The note is `kb/theory/a-citation-cannot-assert-more-fidelity-than-its-capture-preserved.md` in this repository; its text is <Inputs: note.md>. The criterion is `kb/instructions/critique-note.md`; its text is <Inputs: criterion.md>. Judge these input texts; the files on disk may have changed since.

Reading scope:
- The note's relative links resolve from `kb/theory/`. For grounding or consistency checks, read only files the note links to, except for one exact local path that the criterion explicitly tells you to derive from such a link.

Output:

# Critique: A citation cannot assert more fidelity than its capture preserved

**Note:** kb/theory/a-citation-cannot-assert-more-fidelity-than-its-capture-preserved.md
**Central commitment:** A citation's fidelity is capped by the capture layer that holds the passage (verbatim, paraphrase or second-hand). The cap is fixed at ingest and never rises downstream. Notation cannot raise it; only re-capture can.
**Critique mode:** claim
**Attack outcome:** partially lands

## Strongest case against it

The opponent is a provenance engineer from reproducible-research and records-management practice, such as an archivist or the designer of a citation checker that runs against PDFs. They accept the narrow mechanism: writing `verbatim` beside a paraphrase does not make it verbatim. They reject the claim built around it. The note identifies "the capture" with the LLM-facing markdown snapshot. It then treats that snapshot's lossiness as the ceiling on every citation. Those are two different artifacts:

1. **The forcing argument covers only the consumer view.** The context window is a limit on what the LLM reads. Mechanical verification of a quote does not run in the context window; a substring test over extracted PDF text costs nothing there. The note already names the authoritative artifact ("the sibling PDF"), and the KB keeps full external copies in private snapshots. A design can therefore keep layered excerpts for the reader and retain full text as the check's ground truth. That is a boundary-preserving rival in the sense of the linked rival-test note. That note also says that failing to find a rival "certifies nothing", so it cannot support "the layering is not a design choice" even if no rival had been found.

2. **The ceiling is not fixed at ingest.** While the authoritative artifact is retained, a citation can quote it directly with a page locator, and a checker can verify the quote. The note's answer is that this is "re-capture". But if every operation that raises fidelity is renamed re-capture, "only re-capture raises fidelity" becomes true by definition. The substantive claim is then that fidelity is bounded by the most faithful retained ground truth reachable from the citation. That is precondition 3 of the derived-copy rule, a recomputable regime. It is not the history note's regime, in which the record is gone after production. The analogy to "history has one chance to become checkable" fits only when the original is not retained (dead URLs, unretained PDFs, intermediaries). Those are the second-hand cases, not long sources in general.

3. **The corollary contradicts the rule it relies on.** Within one file, layer is a function of position. If the snapshot marks its layers, a layer field in the locator is a derived copy of recomputable truth. The derived-copy rule says to check such a copy or omit it, not to require it in every locator.

On this view the note has a true local mechanism: a marker cannot upgrade the stratum it points into. But it presents that as a temporal law ("fixed at ingest", "one chance") and an inherited constraint ("forced"), and neither generalization survives retention of the authoritative artifact.

## How the note engages it

**Partially engaged.**

- Section "Why notation cannot repair it" fully answers the narrow version: no mechanical derivation rule links paraphrase to source, so a marker cannot move the bound. The attack concedes this.
- The opening paragraph ("The only operation that raises fidelity is re-capture") and the history paragraph ("recoverable only by returning to the authoritative artifact and capturing again") recognize the retained-artifact route. They file it as re-capture without noticing that this weakens "fixed at ingest" and "non-increasing" from a temporal claim to a claim about which ground truth the citation points at.
- Section "Capture is layered because it is forced to be" does not consider separating the LLM-facing snapshot from the verification ground truth. It also reverses the one-way logic of the rival-test note it cites.
- Section "Scope" handles short sources, where layers collapse. It does not handle long sources whose full text is retained for mechanical checking, which is the case the attack targets.
- The corollary does not engage the redundancy objection.

## Constructive findings

- Restate the central bound relative to the retained ground truth: "a citation's fidelity is bounded by the most faithful retained artifact it can be checked against". Make "fixed at ingest" a special case that holds when the authoritative artifact is not retained.
- Limit "forced" to the LLM-facing snapshot. Then either state the boundary invariant that excludes keeping out-of-context full text for verification, or present that design as the rival it is. Do not cite the rival-test note as certifying inheritance.
- Keep the history-note link only for the unretained or second-hand case. Elsewhere, link the claim to the derived-copy rule's precondition 3.
- Rewrite the corollary as "the layer must be resolvable from the locator: either derived from a layer-marked snapshot or encoded and validated". Drop the impossible same-offset example.
- Update the notation paragraph for ADR 046: a paraphrase marked `verbatim` is now a checked false copy that fails validation. It no longer survives as a trusted unchecked copy.
- Describe the ADR 046 mismatches accurately (editorial quoting edits). Alternatively, add evidence that paraphrase-layer passages were marked verbatim, if such evidence exists in the casebook corpus.

## Secondary objections (optional)

- "the two move in opposite directions": fidelity is non-increasing and authority is earned upward. That is a ceiling with growth beneath it, as the note's next sentence says, not opposite motion. The phrase overstates the contrast.
- The second Open Question (fidelity versus usefulness) concedes that the bound constrains verification, not the citation's value to a reader. The title's "cannot assert more fidelity" is safe on that reading. The opening claim that a claim "can be no better grounded than the capture step left it" conflates grounding with fidelity, which the authority paragraph had just separated.

description: Experimental report method that decomposes a note's central commitment into the premises it rests on and hunts a counterexample for each, routing failures as local (revise a premise) or global (the commitment fails)

# Decompose a note into premises and counterexample each

Experimental. This method tests the **nodes** of a note's argument — the premises its central commitment takes as given — not the edges between them. It assumes every stated inference is valid and asks a different question: is each premise the commitment rests on *itself* true, or does a concrete counterexample defeat it? This is the "explanation as a falsification surface" move — a commitment is only as strong as the weakest premise it silently assumes. It is **not a catalog gate** and gives no verdict. It is a report criterion: run it alone with `commonplace-review run gates NOTE --criteria premises`, which writes its review result. Write the report; do not touch the note.

Unlike [reconstruct a note's composition friction](./composition-friction-gate.md), which tests whether each *inference* holds (the edges), this tests whether each *premise* holds (the nodes). The two are complementary: an argument can have valid inferences resting on a false premise, which the friction check passes and this check catches. Run both when a commitment must be load-bearing.

Run it in a **fresh sub-agent**, a different runner than wrote the note, so the checker has no sympathy for the note's framing. Separation is what gives the check teeth: the runner that assumed a premise while writing will assume it again while reading.

The caller owns reviewer lifecycle. After the report has been written and verified, close, terminate, or release the checker with the harness lifecycle operation. The checker is a single-use context and must not receive follow-up work.

## The hard rule

Do **not** emit an overall "sound / unsound" or pass/fail verdict, and do not accept the note. The product is **routed attention**: the premises that a counterexample defeats or dents, and — for each — whether its failure is local or global. **Default to `DOUBTFUL` when uncertain.** A premise earns `HOLDS` only when an active counterexample hunt fails; do not extend it the benefit of the doubt the way fluent reading does.

## Step 1 — State the central commitment

State the note's central commitment in **one sentence**. Match its artifact kind:

- **claim** — the proposition the note asserts is true;
- **definition** — the boundary it draws and asserts is the right cut;
- **procedure** — the outcome it asserts following the steps produces.

## Step 2 — Decompose into load-bearing premises

Enumerate the premises the commitment **rests on and takes as given** — including background premises the note treats as obvious and never argues for. What counts as a premise follows the artifact kind:

- **claim** — a proposition that must be true for the claim to hold;
- **definition** — a commitment that makes this the correct boundary (that the distinguished cases differ in the way named, that the distinction is not idle, that nothing important is mis-sorted);
- **procedure** — an assumption under which the steps produce the intended outcome (about inputs, the executor, the environment, or the world).

List the premises the *argument consumes*, not every true sentence in the note. A premise the note never states but the commitment cannot survive without is the most valuable to surface.

## Step 3 — Counterexample each premise

For each premise, actively hunt a concrete **counterexample** or a specific reason it could be false — a case, input, or situation in which the premise does not hold. Record per premise:

- `HOLDS` — an active hunt found no defeater;
- `DOUBTFUL` — a plausible reason or edge case dents it (state it);
- `DEFEATED` — a concrete counterexample makes it false (state it).

Counterexample by artifact kind: for a claim, a case where the premise is false; for a definition, a case the boundary mis-sorts (over- or under-includes) or a distinction that changes nothing; for a procedure, a situation where the assumption fails and the steps misfire.

**Read each premise at its stated modality** (`kb/theory/COLLECTION.md`, "Claim modality"). A premise stated as a tendency ("usually", "most", "under conditions C") is dented or defeated only by prevalence-shaped evidence — the exceptions being common or the ordinary case going the other way — never by one instance it already concedes. A premise stated as a first-order model with adequacy commitments is attacked through those commitments — an exception its domain treats as ordinary unmarked practice, or the model losing dominance — not by conceded, accounted-for exceptions. A premise with no stated mode reads as universal, and one counterexample others can check again defeats it: a specified case whose conflict with the premise any reader can re-derive, or an observed effect shown to recur. A single unrepeated report of an exception makes the premise `DOUBTFUL`, not `DEFEATED`. When a counterexample defeats a premise only under the conditions the note applied it to, say whether the premise or those conditions fail. The modes differ in the inference form of the refuter: deductive for universal (one checkable instance, modus tollens), inductive for statistical (a sample-based prevalence result), comparative for ideal-type (loss of dominance to the corrections or a rival, or an exception ordinary in its own domain) — hunt each premise's defeater in its mode's form.

For every non-`HOLDS` premise, also record the **counterexample shape**: `instance` (one concrete case), `prevalence` (evidence the exception is common or ordinary), or `priced-exception` (the case is marked, fenced, or charged for in its own domain). The shape is routing information for whoever repairs the note — a prevalence-shaped defeat of a universal premise points at a statistical reframe, and a priced-exception defeat points at an ideal-type candidate — not a verdict, and not this method's call to make.

## Step 4 — Route each failure local or global

For every `DOUBTFUL` or `DEFEATED` premise, classify the scope of its failure:

- **LOCAL** — the failure defeats only this premise; the central commitment can still stand on the remaining premises or be rescued by a qualification (narrow the scope, add a condition). The revision changes a premise and keeps the commitment; the qualification belongs in the note's `## Scope` (or `## Caveats`) section, where a later edit can narrow it further without touching the claim.
- **GLOBAL** — the failure propagates to the central commitment, so the commitment itself fails as stated. The revision must weaken, rescope, or retire the commitment, not just patch a premise.

A `GLOBAL` failure on a load-bearing premise is the strongest signal this method produces; surface it first.

## Output

The caller names the output file. Write only that file; mutate nothing else. The output is a [review result](../types/review-result.md) fragment with `outcome: report` and no `attack-outcome`.

Each premise is one finding, global failures first. Give a premise the note states `scope: passage` with a quote that identifies one span; give an unstated premise `scope: document` with no quotes. Begin its `reason` with `HOLDS`, `DOUBTFUL` or `DEFEATED`, then state the premise at its stated modality and the counterexample or reason. A non-`HOLDS` reason also names `LOCAL` or `GLOBAL` and the shape `instance`, `prevalence` or `priced-exception`. The body explains the decomposition without repeating each finding.

```markdown
---
type: types/review-result.md
findings:
  - scope: document
    quotes: []
    reason: "DOUBTFUL — <premise, at its stated modality> — <the counterexample or reason> — LOCAL — instance"
outcome: report
---

# Premise decomposition: <note title>

**Register:** claim | definition | procedure
**Central commitment (one sentence):** <...>

## Premises and counterexamples
<how the commitment decomposes and why these are the premises it consumes; the premises themselves are the findings>

## For the human
<one line: the premise to look at first — the global defeater if any, else the load-bearing doubtful premise most worth the author's attention>
```

# A citation cannot assert more fidelity than its capture preserved

A claim that cites a captured source can be no better grounded than the capture step left it. Fidelity is fixed at ingest and is **non-increasing** downstream: no citation syntax, no locator type, no review gate can promote a passage to a grade its capture did not preserve. The only operation that raises fidelity is re-capture.

This is a claim about **fidelity**, not authority, and the two move in opposite directions — worth stating plainly, because [trace-extracted memory earns authority per operation, not at capture](./trace-extracted-memory-earns-authority-per-operation-not-at-capture.md) asserts the complement. *Authority* — how much weight a reader should give a claim — is earned by post-capture work: verify, abstract, consult. *Fidelity* — what grade of provenance evidence a passage carries, whether the source's own words or somebody's restatement — is spent at capture and never replenished. The two compose: capture sets a ceiling, and post-capture operations earn authority beneath it. A heavily verified rule can still rest on a second-hand passage; a pristine verbatim quote can sit unverified indefinitely.

## Capture is layered because it is forced to be

The layering is not a design choice — [a framework rule with a boundary-preserving rival is not an inherited constraint](./a-framework-rule-with-a-boundary-preserving-rival-is-not-inherited.md), and no rival capture design drops the layering while preserving the commitments the framework has already made. A long source cannot be captured verbatim into markdown at full fidelity, because the consumer's context window is finite and because copyright forces trims. Any framework whose consumer is an LLM and whose sources are real documents faces both; hosted providers' output filters on mass verbatim reproduction add a third barrier, but that one is provider-contingent rather than inherited. So a snapshot of a long source is not a copy — it is an *extraction*, and it stratifies:

- **Verbatim layer** — the source's own words, reproduced. A claim may quote, and a machine can string-match the quote back against the snapshot.
- **Paraphrase layer** — the snapshot's own-words summary of a passage. A claim may cite it, but must not use quotation marks, and verification requires going back to the authoritative artifact (the sibling PDF).
- **Second-hand** — the captured text is itself another party's restatement (a court restating a complaint; a news article quoting an order whose original is no longer served). The citation must name the intermediary, because the provenance chain has a party in the middle whose fidelity is an assumption.

## Why notation cannot repair it

The temptation is to fix provenance downstream — a richer citation format, a structured span locator, a stricter gate. It cannot work, and the reason is exact rather than merely practical. [A derived copy of recomputable truth must be checked or absent](./a-derived-copy-of-recomputable-truth-must-be-checked-or-absent.md) requires a *mechanical derivation rule* before a copy may be trusted. A verbatim-layer quote has one: substring match. A paraphrase-layer passage has no such rule — there is no mechanical comparison between a paraphrase and its source, only judgment. So marking a paraphrase-layer passage `verbatim` does not make it verbatim; it produces precisely the hand-maintained-and-trusted copy that rule forbids, with a stronger trust signal attached than the unmarked version would carry. Notation can *express* the fidelity bound. It cannot move it.

This is the citation-fidelity instance of a general rule: [history has one chance to become checkable](./history-has-one-chance-to-become-checkable.md). The one chance here is ingest, and what was not preserved verbatim then is permanently downgraded — recoverable only by returning to the authoritative artifact and capturing again.

## Corollary: a locator must carry the layer, not just the span

It follows that a source-span locator encoding only *position* is underspecified. **Two spans at the same file offset can differ in provenance quality by a full layer** — one lifted from the snapshot's verbatim block, one from its paraphrase summary. A position-only locator would render them identical, which is the one distinction a consumer of the citation most needs. Any locator design must encode the layer.

## Scope

Change the premise and the conclusion moves, which is where the claim earns its boundaries. If a source is short enough to capture losslessly — a tweet, a short abstract, a commit message — the layers collapse to one, the bound goes vacuous, and *position* becomes the binding constraint again. In that regime a structured span locator earns its keep; the corollary above is out of scope rather than in conflict with that design. The claim bites exactly where capture is lossy, which is to say wherever the sources are long.

The practical consequence is that provenance quality is decided *before any note is written*. If a passage will be load-bearing, it must be promoted into the snapshot's verbatim layer at capture time, or the author must return to the authoritative artifact and quote-mine it. Because the debt is fixed at ingest and visible in the citation, it can at least be made explicit and repaid deliberately rather than discovered later.

## Open Questions

- Does forum-thread or transcript sourcing — many small utterances rather than a few long papers — change the natural grain, since each utterance *is* losslessly capturable while the corpus is not?
- Fidelity is a ceiling on verification, but is it a ceiling on *usefulness*? A well-attributed paraphrase may serve a reader better than a verbatim fragment shorn of context.

---

Evidence for the layering and for the failure of naive `verbatim` marking comes from both epistack casebook work in the sibling `epistack-casebooks` repository and from [ADR 046](../reference/adr/046-verbatim-quotes-are-validated-against-their-cited-source.md): the shipped verbatim-quote checker, run over that corpus, found eighteen of eighty-seven `verbatim`-marked spans that did not appear in their cited snapshot, with no false mismatches on manual audit.

# Writing conventions for kb/reports/ (report collection)

## Purpose and scope

This collection contains analytical outputs, evaluation records, and local
operational evidence that are consumed as reports rather than as library
claims or system definitions. Placement here is justified by the output's
retention policy and consumer, not by its filename or by the fact that a tool
generated it.

A report belongs here only when a named operation consumes the report itself.
Transferable claims belong in `kb/theory/`; descriptions of the shipped system
and its decisions belong in `kb/reference/`; executable procedures belong in
`kb/instructions/`; and reasoning whose value is consumed by unfinished work
belongs in `kb/work/`.

## Policy areas

Every report artifact lives in exactly one first-level policy area:

| Area | Retention policy | Typical contents |
|---|---|---|
| `state/` | Ignored, one directory per producing workflow. Not disposable merely because it was generated: the owning workflow decides when an output may be removed, and the [state README](./state/README.md) states per workflow what deletion loses. | Review results, packets and runs; fix dispositions; ingest working directories; connect, critique, friction, premise-decomposition and promotion-candidate reports. |
| `retained/` | Durable report records kept with the project. Payloads are tracked. | Evaluation corpora, experiment reports, measurements, and exact records cited by later work. |
| `types/` | Collection-local structural contracts, not report payloads. | Optional project-authored report contracts; command-produced generic report types are global. |

The published site includes `retained/` and leaves out `state/`. Inside `retained/`, a subtree carrying a
`.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker is left out of the site as well as
validation; mark exact captures and trial bundles so, keeping the report that
interprets them published.

Do not put report payloads directly at the collection root. Moving an artifact
between policy areas is a change in its retention contract, not a filing-only
rename.

## Quality goal

Make the report sufficient for the operation that consumes it without making
it impersonate a durable knowledge claim. State the subject, inputs or source
state, method, result, and material limits to the degree needed to interpret
or reproduce the output. Record the model and prompt or instruction identity
when an LLM judgment is part of the evidence and the producing workflow does
not already retain them.

`state/` must satisfy the owning workflow's authority, integrity, and cleanup
rules. `retained/` must remain
understandable from a clean checkout without relying on ignored files.

## Titles, descriptions, and exact records

- Use a title that names the analysis, experiment, or result. A title such as
  "Report" does not distinguish the artifact.
- When frontmatter is present, write a retrieval-oriented `description` that
  identifies the subject and why the exact output is retained.
- Frontmatter-free Markdown is permitted for deliberate unstructured output.
- Preserve an exact capture when fidelity is the report's purpose. If a copied
  artifact carries another collection's local type only as captured data, put
  a `.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker at the capture-set root rather than
  presenting that copy as a live typed artifact of this collection.

## Maintenance semantics

- A state producer owns cleanup and states, in the state README, what deleting
  its output loses: nothing unique (rebuild from retained inputs), one paid
  judgment (rerun when needed) or current coverage, an unresolved disposition
  or decision evidence (preserve). Generated state may contain non-reproducible
  judgments or the only current disposition, so Git ignore status never
  licenses deletion.
- A retained report is changed according to its declared role. Correct a
  living report in place; preserve a dated or frozen observation as an exact
  record and create a new observation when the measured state changes.
- Local evidence notes are the one interpreted form `retained/` keeps as
  durable artifacts: a `types/note.md` artifact whose bounded inference
  concerns only Commonplace's own choices or their measured effects, beside
  the raw records it interprets. Its formal edges use this collection's labels
  below. An inference that keeps a free variable belongs in
  `kb/theory/evidence/`.
- If a report develops a transferable claim, binding rule, system premise, or
  unfinished-work lifecycle, extract that content to its proper collection.
  Do not broaden `retained/` into a second notes, reference, instructions, or
  workshop collection.

## Outbound links

Reports may inspect any project surface. Use relative Markdown links for live
navigation and state in prose why the target matters. Inline links may carry
ordinary evidential or procedural context. Footer-shaped formal edges use this
small authorized set:

| label | destinations | reader need |
|---|---|---|
| `derived-from` | sources, external | inspect the source material from which the report was produced |
| `is-evidence-for` | theory, reference, reports | inspect the durable claim, decision, or report record on which this output bears |
| `compares-with` | theory, reference, sources, reports | compare two artifacts on a named shared axis |
| `see-also` | any durable collection, external | inspect useful adjacent context when no stronger relation applies |

The destination collection separately decides whether it may author a
reciprocal edge. A formal edge into this collection targets `retained/`;
`state/` may be mentioned inline only as local operational context.

Tracked library artifacts must not depend on an ignored `state/` file being
present. Summarize the needed evidence in the tracked artifact or
promote the exact report to `retained/` first. Tracked artifacts may cite a
`retained/` report when the exact record is useful to their reader.

## Validation markers

The tracked `.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker at `state/` excludes its
data-bearing subtree from collection-scoped validation. The marker does not
hide files from ordinary discovery, and explicit validation of
one typed report still applies its type contract.

A file under `state/` may declare any valid type spec, including another
collection's local type. Workflows stage candidates there for other
collections, and a candidate must validate against its destination's contract.
The type spec itself stays in the owning collection's `types/` directory.
`retained/` does not share this exception.

## What does not belong here

- A generated explanation or synthesis whose claim should survive the run →
  `kb/theory/` or `kb/reference/` according to its consumer.
- A procedure named "report" because it produces one → `kb/instructions/`.
- Drafts, deliberation, and run traces consumed by an unfinished investigation
  → `kb/work/`.
- External source captures and their durable analyses → `kb/sources/`.
- Build outputs with no report consumer → their build cache, not `kb/reports/`.

# Review result

A review result records one assessment of captured target text against a criterion. Completion means the output passed deterministic checks, not that its judgment is correct. A report outcome is not a favorable verdict. Use this type for individual gate, compression-check, type-conformance and collection-conformance verdicts, and for critique, composition-friction, premise-decomposition and compression-synthesis reports and role reports. Do not use it for combined improvement packets or connection discovery.

## Content

Findings state what the assessed text establishes or fails to establish. Each passage finding quotes enough verbatim text to identify one contiguous span uniquely. A quote is matched after whitespace and typographic quote marks are normalized, so a line wrap in the target does not break it. A quote therefore identifies a passage and is not a byte-exact copy of it. A consumer that needs the exact span locates the quote in the captured target, which holds the exact bytes. A document-wide or absence finding explains the condition without inventing a quotation. Finding levels belong to verdict criteria; critique reports instead state whether the strongest attack lands and how the note engages it. An empty findings list is an honest completed result when no finding remains.

The body explains the assessment without repeating every structured finding. A critique preserves its central commitment, critique mode, strongest case, the note's response and constructive findings, including why an attack does not survive. Low-confidence no-surviving-attack findings leave the need for a domain check visible.

Each report method has its own shape, which the schema checks by the result's `criterion`:

| Method | Findings | Required body |
|---|---|---|
| Critique | constructive findings | `attack-outcome` in frontmatter; `## Strongest case against it`, `## How the note engages it`, `## Constructive findings` |
| Composition friction | the surfaced joints, thinnest first; each reason begins `UNSUPPORTED`, `THIN` or `HOLDS` | a `**Filter:** SURVIVES` or `DISSOLVES` line; `## Filter`, `## Thinnest joints`, `## For the human` |
| Premise decomposition | one per premise; each reason begins `HOLDS`, `DOUBTFUL` or `DEFEATED`, and a non-`HOLDS` reason names `LOCAL` or `GLOBAL` and `instance`, `prevalence` or `priced-exception` | a `**Register:**` line; `## Premises and counterexamples`, `## For the human` |
| Compression synthesis | zero to three opportunities | `## Opportunities` |
| Role report | one per dependent need, duplication or untaken recommendation; each reason begins `SUPPLIED`, `PARTLY SUPPLIED`, `NOT SUPPLIED`, `DUPLICATED` or `UNTAKEN` | `## Role`, `## Dependents`, `## Duplication`, `## Untaken recommendations`, `## Reach` |

Only critique supplies `attack-outcome`. Friction's filter line and the premise statuses route attention; they are not overall verdicts. A report criterion is named by its library instruction's identity, so moving one of these instructions requires a schema edit.

## Field ownership

The worker fragment supplies only `type`, `findings`, `outcome`, optional `attack-outcome`, and the body. Findings precede the outcome so the serialized verdict follows its rationale. The fragment is not a complete saved artifact. The controller completes and validates it; workers never assert hashes, execution identities or timestamps.

| Fields | Owner and meaning |
|---|---|
| `type`, `findings`, `outcome`, `attack-outcome` | Worker assessment; findings contain `scope`, `quotes`, `reason`, and `level` for verdicts |
| `description`, `format`, `contract` | Controller's result-format identity and expected verdict/report contract |
| `note`, `criterion` | Original target and criterion identities |
| `note-sha256`, `criterion-sha256` | Freshness hashes; the note hash may cover normalized watched parts, not exact bytes |
| `target-sha256`, `target-capture` | Exact assessed UTF-8 bytes and their retained repository-relative location |
| `observation`, `contract-sha256` | Execution observation and captured output-contract identity |
| `profile`, `model`, `run`, `launch`, `completed-at` | Requested execution configuration and observed execution provenance |
| `raw-output`, `raw-output-sha256` | Retained original worker fragment, distinct from this completed artifact |

## Template

Worker fragment for a verdict criterion; code supplies the remaining fields:

```markdown
---
type: types/review-result.md
findings:
  - scope: document
    quotes: []
    reason: "The claim omits the condition needed for its stated conclusion."
    level: warn
outcome: warn
---

# Review

## Summary

The conclusion needs its missing condition.
```

A critique fragment uses `outcome: report`, supplies `attack-outcome`, and omits finding levels. Its body retains the critique instruction's sections. Other report fragments use `outcome: report`, omit `attack-outcome` and finding levels, and follow their instruction's Output section. Neither fragment uses a terminal `## Result:` line. Operational production and publication belong to the review command, not to this type.

request.task:
Review one note against one criterion. Nobody will answer questions. If you cannot judge the pair, write <the problem file named at the end of this invocation> instead of guessing.

The note is `kb/theory/a-citation-cannot-assert-more-fidelity-than-its-capture-preserved.md` in this repository; its text is <Inputs: note.md>. The criterion is `kb/instructions/premise-decomposition-gate.md`; its text is <Inputs: criterion.md>. Judge these input texts; the files on disk may have changed since.

Reading scope:
- The note's relative links resolve from `kb/theory/`. For grounding or consistency checks, read only files the note links to, except for one exact local path that the criterion explicitly tells you to derive from such a link.
- Ignore review backups, workshop copies and historical artifacts unless the note links to them.
- Never browse shared operational state or other runs, even through a link. Operational inputs must be supplied copies.
- Do not delegate or start another agent.

Output:
- Write the review to <Required outputs: review.md>. Write nothing else: create, edit or delete no file in the repository, and run no command that changes it or its git state.
- Write YAML frontmatter with type: types/review-result.md, findings, then outcome: report. No attack-outcome.
- Findings have scope, quotes and reason, but no severity level. The criterion's Output section says what each
  finding holds and how its reason begins. An empty list is allowed.
- Write the body the criterion's Output section describes, with its required sections.
- Use the supplied review-result contract. Supply only worker-owned fields. No terminal Result footer.

argv: Read the complete invocation at `{prompt}` and follow it. Recover any truncated read before proceeding.
